content: Latin, known as lingua Latīna, is an ancient Indo-European language that was originally spoken in Ancient Rome. It served as the de facto international language of science and scholarship in much of Europe until the 17th century. Through Roman conquests, Latin spread across the Mediterranean and much of Europe, later evolving into the Romance languages spoken in regions such as France, Italy, Romania, and the Iberian Peninsula. These languages, in turn, were carried to the Americas and Africa through colonization. Latin is traditionally divided into two forms: Classical Latin, which was used in poetry and formal prose, and Vulgar Latin, a collection of spoken dialects that eventually diverged into the Romance languages. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the rise of the Catholic Church, Latin became the ecclesiastical language of the Church and the lingua franca of the educated classes in the West. By the 16th century, Latin began to decline as a spoken language, though Vulgar Latin persisted in regional dialects, which by the 9th century had evolved into the ancestors of modern Romance languages. Ecclesiastical Latin remains in use within the Catholic Church, and Latin vocabulary continues to be employed in fields such as science, academia, and law. Classical Latin, the literary language of the late Roman Republic and early Empire, is still taught in many schools, often alongside Greek in the study of Classics. However, its prominence has diminished since the early 20th century. The Latin alphabet, with its modern variants such as the English, Spanish, and French alphabets, is the most widely used writing system in the world. Historically, Latin is a member of the Italic language family, and its alphabet is derived from the Old Italic script, which in turn was based on the Greek alphabet. Latin was introduced to the Italian peninsula in the 9th or 8th century BCE by the migrating Latins, who settled in Latium around the River Tiber, where Roman civilization later developed. During its early years, Latin was influenced by the non-Indo-European Etruscan language of northern Italy. While surviving Roman literature is predominantly in Classical Latin, the spoken language of the Western Roman Empire among ordinary people was Vulgar Latin, which differed from Classical Latin in grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation. Although Latin remained the legal and governmental language of the Roman Empire, Greek was the dominant language of the educated elite, as much of the literature and philosophy studied by upper-class Romans was produced by Greek authors, particularly those from Athens. In the Eastern Roman Empire, which became the Byzantine Empire after the final split of the Eastern and Western Empires in 395 CE, Greek eventually supplanted Latin as the legal and governmental language and had long been the lingua franca of most Eastern citizens. The Romans used the Latin alphabet, derived from the Old Italic script, to write their language. This alphabet survives today as the writing system for Romance, Celtic, Germanic (including English), and many other languages. Ancient Romans did not use punctuation, macrons (though they occasionally used marks to distinguish between long and short vowels), the letters J and U, lowercase letters (though they had a cursive script), or interword spacing (dots were sometimes placed between words to aid readability). Roman cursive script is commonly found on wax tablets excavated at sites such as Vindolanda on Hadrian's Wall in Britain. The expansion of the Roman Empire spread Latin throughout Europe. Over time, Vulgar Latin began to diverge into distinct Romance languages, a process well underway by the 9th century. These languages were initially oral, with Latin remaining the primary written language. For example, Latin was the official language of Portugal until 1296, when it was replaced by Portuguese. Many Romance languages, including Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, and Romanian, flourished, with differences between them becoming more pronounced over time. Italian is the most conservative descendant of Latin in terms of vocabulary, while Sardinian is the most conservative in terms of phonology. Some differences between Classical Latin and the Romance languages have been used to reconstruct Vulgar Latin. For instance, Romance languages exhibit distinctive stress patterns, whereas Latin had both stress and distinctive vowel length. Italian and Sardinian retain distinctive consonant length as well as stress, while Spanish and Portuguese retain only stress. French, for most speakers, has lost both distinctive length and stress. Another major distinction is that most Romance languages, except Romanian, have lost case endings in most words, retaining them only in some pronouns. Romanian retains a direct case (nominative/accusative), an indirect case (dative/genitive), a vocative, and is the only Romance language to preserve the neuter gender and at least partial declension from Latin. Latin has also had a significant influence on English. While English is Germanic in grammar, much of its vocabulary is derived from Latin, often indirectly through Anglo-Norman and French. Approximately 60% of English vocabulary has Latin roots. During the medieval period, much of this borrowing occurred through ecclesiastical usage established by Saint Augustine of Canterbury in the 6th century or indirectly after the Norman Conquest via Anglo-Norman. From the 16th to the 18th centuries, English writers coined numerous new words from Latin and Greek roots, often referred to as inkhorn terms. While many of these words fell out of use, others, such as imbibe, extrapolate, dormant, and employer, became integral to the language. Latin mottos are still used by many organizations as guiding principles. The largest organization that continues to use Latin in official contexts is the Roman Catholic Church. Although the Mass of Paul VI is usually celebrated in the local vernacular, it is often said in Latin, particularly in the Vatican. Latin is also used in scientific nomenclature for organisms, where linguistic neutrality is preferred. Films such as Sebastiane and The Passion of the Christ have been produced with dialogue in Latin. Many organizations today have Latin mottos, such as Semper fidelis (always faithful), the motto of the United States Marine Corps. Some universities still hold graduation ceremonies in Latin. Latin is a synthetic, fusional language, meaning that affixes (often suffixes) are attached to fixed stems to express grammatical categories such as gender, number, and case in nouns, pronouns, and adjectives—a process known as declension. Similarly, affixes are attached to verb stems to denote person, number, tense, voice, mood, and aspect—a process called conjugation. Latin nouns have six main cases: nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, and ablative, with a seventh, the locative case, used to indicate location. These cases determine a noun's syntactic role in a sentence, making word order less important than in languages like English. Latin verbs are categorized into four main conjugations, each with distinct inflectional patterns. There are six general tenses (present, imperfect, future, perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect), four grammatical moods (indicative, infinitive, imperative, and subjunctive), six persons (first, second, and third, each in singular and plural), two voices (active and passive), and a few aspects. Verbs are described by four principal parts, which provide the forms needed to conjugate the verb in all tenses and moods. Instruction in Latin, particularly in secondary schools and universities, focuses primarily on translating Latin texts into modern languages rather than on oral communication. This approach emphasizes reading and writing skills while de-emphasizing speaking and listening. Understanding the sounds of Latin words can provide insight into how ancient authors spoke and incorporated stylistic elements into their works, particularly in poetry and literature. Latin continues to influence modern culture and education. Many international auxiliary languages have been heavily influenced by Latin. For example, Interlingua is sometimes considered a simplified, modern version of Latin. Latin translations of modern literature, such as Paddington Bear, Winnie the Pooh, Tintin, Asterix, Harry Potter, and The Cat in the Hat, aim to sustain interest in the language. Latin terms are also used in isolation as technical terms in fields such as medicine and law.
